title: The four truths, now
hookLine: dukkha, its cause, its end, the path, as you understand them now
tomorrow: why did the Buddha give brahmins a road to Brahma?

lines: A FEW LEAVES IN HIS HAND.
cards: A grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi, leaves underfoot and leaves overhead. The Buddha was staying there with his monks.
He bent down, picked up a few fallen leaves, held them out to the monks, and asked: which are more, these leaves in my hand, or the leaves in the trees above us? The ones above, they said. Many more.
So it is, he told them, with what I've known and not taught you. So which few leaves did he keep in his hand?

teach.b: His answer, in the Samyutta Nikaya, is plain. He left the rest untaught because it didn't help: it didn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. What he did teach was four things.
This is dukkha: the ache in things, the way even good things won't hold still. This is its arising: craving, the thirst that keeps wanting more, or wanting other.
This is its ending: when the thirst lets go, the ache ends with it, and Buddhists call that nirvana.

And this is the path to its ending: the noble eightfold path. These are the four noble truths, and the suttas put them at the heart of his first sermon, to five companions in the deer park near Benares.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says them in one breath: "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain."
Some teachers read the four like a doctor's visit: what's wrong, what's causing it, can it end, and the treatment.
Read that way, the first three point at the fourth.

That's why the line today says one path. The handful hasn't grown in five years. What this path has added is the walking: the breath, the precepts, the sits, the kindness, each one a piece of the fourth.

how: The four noble truths are taught to beginners in Buddhist temples and centers, chanted in Pali in some, and studied again and again over a lifetime.

o: four vows a monk speaks on his first morning
the ache, its cause, its ending, and the path out
four facts about karma and the next life

games.q: four leaves in the hand — tap the pairs.
p: craving, the thirst for more or other

s: the first truth says life is nothing but misery
it names dukkha, the ache in things that won't hold still. the third truth says it can end.
the Buddha said he knew more than he taught
the leaves overhead were many more than the few in his hand; he taught what helps.
the four truths are four separate facts to memorize
read like a doctor's visit, the first three point at the fourth: the path.

games.q: a friend says, 'Buddhism is just pessimism: life is suffering, the end.' which part of the four truths answers that best?
o: the third and fourth: the ache can end, and there's a path to it.
the first: if you look closely, the ache isn't really there at all.
the second: craving is good, because it keeps people going.
games.why: the Buddha didn't stop at dukkha. the third truth is its ending, and the fourth is the way there.

practice: Pick up four small things near you, leaves if you have them, or coins, or pens.
Lay them in your open palm one at a time, and as each one lands, name a truth in your own words, as if to someone across a kitchen table: the ache, its cause, its ending, the way.
Then close your hand gently and sit with the fourth.

wordCard.voice: The four truths: dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the path. The handful of leaves the Buddha chose to keep in his hand.

orig.note: Pali: the four noble truths, cattari ariyasaccani.

carryVoice: Keep this one: four truths, one path, and the path is the part you walk. Nine days up the summit.
